**Self-RAG — moving the retrieval decision out of the prompt and into the weights (2023–2024)**

The controller in this lesson is a prompt: tool schemas plus a system message telling an LLM to reason, retrieve, judge sufficiency and retrieve again. It works, and it is entirely a runtime construct — the policy lives in text you can edit between requests. In October 2023, Akari Asai, Zeqiu Wu, Yizhong Wang, Avirup Sil and Hannaneh Hajishirzi published Self-RAG (arXiv 2310.11511; ICLR 2024), which took the opposite bet: train the control policy into the generator itself.

Self-RAG expands the model's vocabulary with four reflection tokens. `Retrieve` decides whether the next segment needs evidence, emitting yes, no or continue. `IsRel` judges whether a fetched passage is relevant. `IsSup` judges whether the segment it has written is actually supported by that passage. `IsUse` rates overall utility on a one-to-five scale. Generation runs as a segment-level beam search with beam width 2, ranking candidates by a weighted combination of those token probabilities. Relevance- and support-checking are therefore not separate evaluator calls in a loop — they are logits from the same forward pass.

The results are strong. On PopQA, Self-RAG scores 54.9 at 7B and 55.8 at 13B, against 14.7 for Llama2-13B, 29.3 for ChatGPT and 50.8 for retrieval-augmented ChatGPT; on PubHealth the 13B model reaches 74.5 against ChatGPT's 70.1. The instructive figure is ASQA, where citation precision reaches 70.3 against 65.1 for retrieval-augmented ChatGPT while citation recall is lower, 71.3 against 76.6. The system is not more fluent; it is better at declining to claim support it lacks, and pays for that in coverage.

What it costs is the part worth studying. The generator was trained on 150k instruction-output pairs, labelled by a Llama-7B critic distilled from GPT-4 on roughly 4k to 20k instances per token type. Beam width 2 means each segment is generated more than once. And the policy is frozen into parameters: the only runtime knob left is a threshold on the `Retrieve` probability, and raising it cuts retrieval frequency and accuracy together on knowledge-heavy sets such as PubHealth. A prompt you could rewrite in an afternoon has become a training run.

That is the architectural fork this lesson puts in front of you. A prompted ReAct controller is inspectable, swappable across any model you can call, and cheap to correct when it loops or halts early. A trained controller decides faster, spends no context window on tool schemas, and yields calibrated sufficiency judgements rather than a model's opinion of its own reasoning — but you own a fine-tuning pipeline for as long as the product lives. Settle which you can maintain before you settle how elaborate your loop should be.

**ICIJ — a leak too connected to search (2016–2017)**

The Panama Papers reached the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists as 11.5 million files, 2.6 terabytes, from the law firm Mossack Fonseca. ICIJ's first move was to build an index: Apache Tika and Tesseract, driven by an in-house tool called Extract, turned scans, emails and invoices into machine-readable text, and Apache Solr spread the result across some 30 servers behind a Blacklight interface for the 380-plus journalists in nearly 80 countries. That answered whether a name appeared. It could not answer the question the story turned on.

The leak had two shapes. There were documents, and there was Mossack Fonseca's internal registry — structured records of companies, their officers, the intermediaries who set them up, and registered addresses. ICIJ loaded the registry into Neo4j under four node labels, Entity, Officer, Intermediary and Address, joined by typed edges `OFFICER_OF`, `INTERMEDIARY_OF` and `REGISTERED_ADDRESS`, with Linkurious on top. "Which other companies sit at this address" is one hop here and unaskable of a keyword index. "How is this politician connected to that shell company" becomes `allShortestPaths` across officer, entity and address nodes.

Two model choices matter more than the headline. The published query guide bounds traversal at ten hops: when one registered agent's address is shared by thousands of companies, an unbounded neighbourhood query returns the whole graph. And ICIJ declined to merge duplicates. Instead of collapsing two "John Smith" nodes into one canonical entity — the normalisation step most graph builders treat as routine — the schema carries `SAME_NAME_AS` and `SAME_ID_AS` as separate, deliberately weaker edges. In a newsroom a wrong merge is a libel risk, so ambiguity is handed to the journalist, not resolved by the pipeline.

The second cost was coverage. The graph described the registry, not the correspondence: the public Offshore Leaks database grown from this work holds close to 320,000 offshore entities and more than 360,000 names from 1977 to 2015. Reporters worked the two indices in alternation — traverse the graph for a hypothesis, then return to Solr for the email that evidenced it. That is this lesson's hybrid retrieval layer, with humans doing the merging and ranking.

You make ICIJ's choice the moment you write the extraction prompt. "Normalise entity names to canonical forms" buys clean traversals and quietly fabricates identity claims your sources never made; refusing leaves your retriever with three nodes where the world has one person. Decide before ingest whether your domain punishes a false merge more than a missed link — and if it does, model the ambiguity as an edge and let retrieval, or the reader, settle it.

**ColPali — deleting OCR from the pipeline, and paying for it in storage (2024–2025)**

The orthodox way to index a visually rich PDF is the one this lesson describes: detect layout, OCR the text, caption the figures with a vision-language model, chunk, embed. In July 2024 Manuel Faysse and colleagues published ViDoRe, a page-level retrieval benchmark, alongside ColPali, a model that removes the first three stages (arXiv 2407.01449; ICLR 2025).

The baseline measurements are the interesting part. On an NVIDIA L4, the full Unstructured pipeline took 7.22 seconds per page to index — 0.81s of layout detection, 2.67s of OCR and 3.71s of captioning. Captioning was therefore the most expensive stage in the system. It was also the one that bought nothing: Unstructured plus captioning plus BM25 averaged 65.1 nDCG@5 across ViDoRe, against 65.5 for the same pipeline with plain OCR. Half the indexing budget went on descriptions of figures that left retrieval quality where it started.

ColPali's mechanism is to refuse the lossy step. The page image goes straight into a vision-language model, and rather than pooling to a single vector it keeps a little over a thousand 128-dimensional patch embeddings per page. Scoring is MaxSim late interaction: each query token takes its highest similarity against any patch, and those maxima are summed. A query about a value in a table's third column can land on the patches that draw it, with no intermediate text ever existing. The average across ViDoRe is 81.3 nDCG@5, roughly sixteen points over both text baselines, at 0.39 seconds per page to index.

The bill arrives in the index. Query encoding is a non-issue — about 30 ms against 22 ms for BGE-M3. Storage is not: 257.5 KB per page in float16 versus 8.60 KB for BGE-M3, thirty times the footprint. Nor is scoring free: MaxSim is not one dot product but a query-length by patch-count matrix per candidate page, which does not compose with single-vector ANN indexes the way your stack assumes. The authors observe that compression can cut the footprint by about two orders of magnitude with limited loss — which is a fair way of saying that anyone shipping this owns a pooling and quantisation strategy.

This lesson offers you three ways to get an image into a retrievable index, and they are not interchangeable. Captioning is the one that looks safest, because the output is text and every downstream component already handles text — and it is the one ViDoRe measured as costing the most and returning the least. Direct single-vector embedding is cheap and blurs detail. Multi-vector late interaction wins on quality and moves your cost from indexing time into storage and scoring, permanently. Work out which of those three budgets you actually control before you pick an encoder.

**Jina AI — the chunk was right; the boundary was the bug (2024)**

Take three consecutive sentences from Wikipedia's article on Berlin. The first names the city; the second opens "Its more than 3.85 million inhabitants..."; the third opens "The city is also one of...". Split on sentence boundaries and embed each chunk alone — the standard pipeline — and the two pronoun chunks have lost their antecedent. Scored against a "Berlin" query, cosine similarity is 0.8486 for the sentence naming Berlin but only 0.7084 and 0.7535 for the two that merely refer to it. Both were relevant; the segmentation made them look otherwise.

In September 2024 Michael Günther, Isabelle Mohr, Daniel James Williams, Bo Wang and Han Xiao at Jina AI published "Late Chunking" (arXiv 2409.04701). Their fix changes the order of operations, not the boundaries: run the whole document through a long-context embedding model first, then apply the chunk spans to the resulting token embeddings and mean-pool within each span. Identical text, identical splits — but every token has already attended to the rest of the document. On those Berlin sentences the two pronoun chunks rise to 0.8249 and 0.8498, level with the one that names the city.

The aggregate gains are honest and modest. Averaged across BEIR tasks and three embedding models, nDCG@10 moves from 52.4 to 54.3 with sentence boundaries, 52.2 to 54.0 with fixed-size chunks and 52.4 to 53.8 with semantic boundaries — roughly 2.7 to 3.6 per cent relative. Per dataset: SciFact 0.651 to 0.686, TRECCOVID 0.617 to 0.656, FiQA 0.347 to 0.359.

Two findings matter more than the averages. First, the semantic-boundary variant — the expensive option in this lesson, needing an embedding pass per sentence to locate breakpoints — gained the least of the three. Once the context problem is solved elsewhere, paying for clever boundaries returns less, not more. Second, late chunking lost to naive chunking on the synthetic Needle-8192 and Passkey-8192 sets, where a short relevant fact sits inside unrelated filler: contextualising a chunk with its neighbours dilutes the signal you want when the neighbours are noise. The method is also bounded by the encoder's context window, and offers no benefit past it.

When retrieval misses, the reflex is to hunt for a better boundary — switch to semantic, try agentic splitting, tune the threshold k. Establish first which failure you have. A chunk cut in the wrong place and one cut in the right place but stripped of its referents look identical in a recall metric, and have opposite fixes: the first wants a smarter splitter, the second wants the split moved behind the encoder, or the parent chunk retrieved in place of the child. Diagnose before you buy either — the expensive splitter fixes only the first.

**DoorDash — the verification step that must finish before the courier gives up (2024)**

A Dasher stuck mid-delivery needs an answer now. DoorDash's flow-based automation covered only a narrow set of issues, and the knowledge base behind it was comprehensive but hard to navigate, slow to parse at a doorstep and largely English-only. DoorDash's 2024 engineering account describes the replacement: a RAG-based support assistant over that knowledge base, handling thousands of requests a day.

The retrieval pipeline is unremarkable, which is the point. A multi-turn conversation is summarised to the core issue, similar historical cases and knowledge-base articles are retrieved against that summary, a templated prompt assembles the context, and the model generates. One preprocessing detail is worth stealing: a case-state layer condenses tool history and delivery events into structured context first, so internal system state is not mistaken for something sayable to the Dasher.

What makes it production is what follows generation. Running an LLM evaluator on every reply was cost-prohibitive, so the guardrail is tiered: a cheap semantic-similarity comparison between the drafted response and the retrieved articles runs first, and only failures escalate to a full LLM evaluation of groundedness, conversational coherence and policy compliance. DoorDash reports this reduced hallucinations by 90% and severe compliance issues by 99%. The premise generalises: the model that hallucinates while composing a whole answer is dependable when asked one narrow closed question about an answer already written.

The cost is latency, and how they paid it is the honest part. When guardrail evaluation runs long, the system does not make the Dasher wait — it routes the conversation to a human agent, so the effective automation rate is lower than the quality figures suggest. Offline, an LLM Judge scores transcripts on five dimensions — retrieval correctness, response accuracy, grammar and language accuracy, coherence to context, and relevance to the request — alongside human review of random samples and a regression harness likened to unit tests for prompts. That split is what exposed language drift, which any single aggregate score would have hidden.

Every stage this lesson adds after retrieval — rewriting, re-ranking, citation verification, guardrails — buys quality with milliseconds. Where a person is waiting on a doorstep that budget is fixed: an answer arriving late is a lost automation however correct it was. So fix the number first: decide what your p95 must be, then which verifications are cheap enough for every request, which run only on suspicion, and what happens when time runs out. A diagram that does not say what happens at the deadline is not yet a production design.
